claim: In a 2021 case series study published in JAMA Network Open, 17 of 30 (57%) immune health dietary supplement products purchased from Amazon had inaccurate labels; 13 were misbranded and 9 had unlisted ingredients detected.
stance_target: Amazon supplement quality and labeling accuracy is systematically deficient
scope_conditions: 30 top-featured (4+ star rated) immune health supplements purchased from Amazon in May 2021; tested at University of Mississippi National Center for Natural Products Research using LC-MS
quoted_support: Thirteen of the 30 products had accurate labels based on the product analysis. Of the 17 products with inaccurate labels, 13 had ingredients listed on the labels that were not detected through analysis, such that their labels were misbranded. Additionally, 9 had additional components detected but not claimed on the label.
entities: Uniformed Services University of the Health Sciences

claim: None of the 30 Amazon immune health supplements analyzed in this JAMA study had a recognized third-party certification seal (NSF, USP, BSCG, Informed Sport); 16 products displayed unverified self-promotional 'seals'.
stance_target: Third-party certification is rare among Amazon supplement listings despite being the main quality signal consumers should look for
quoted_support: No product had a third-party certification seal (ie, naming the third-party company), such as BSCG (Banned Substances Control Group), NSF (National Sanitation Foundation) International, Informed Sport, or USP (US Pharmacopeia), presented on the label. Sixteen products had other seals such as '#1 doctor recommended brand,' 'third party tested,' 'purity and potency,' 'stimulant free,' 'lab tested verified,' and 'quality guaranteed.'

claim: The JAMA study's analytical method could NOT verify fat-soluble vitamins including Vitamin D3 — meaning the mislabeling findings apply primarily to botanical/herbal ingredients and water-soluble vitamins, not necessarily to D3.
stance_target: Direct applicability of Amazon mislabeling data to Vitamin D3 supplement quality
scope_conditions: Limitation of LC-MS method used in the 2021 JAMA study
quoted_support: The developed analytical method for product analysis is good for analysis of botanical ingredients, single compounds (synthetic or natural ones), water-soluble vitamins, and amino acids but is not sensitive for analysis of polysaccharides, lipids, enzymes, and proteins. Therefore, elements such as zinc, magnesium, calcium, selenium, probiotic and prebiotic ingredients, mushrooms, and vitamin D3 could not be verified through analysis and therefore are not included as ingredients for analysis.

claim: E-commerce represented 15.1% of the total supplement market in 2020-2021, with 77% of online supplement sales occurring on Amazon.
stance_target: Amazon's role in the supplement market
quoted_support: e-Commerce represents 15.1% of the total supplement market and 77% of supplement sales happen through Amazon.
numbers: 77% of eCommerce supplement sales on Amazon
